segments.text: Apple runs a 3 billion parameter language model right on your iPhone. That's about 3 billion
numbers, called parameters, sitting in the phone's memory. The model summarises text,
pulls out key facts, and sorts things into categories. It does all of that while sharing
the phone with the operating system and whatever apps you've got open. And somehow the phone
doesn't slow down. It doesn't get hot, the battery still makes it past lunch.
So, how did Apple do it? It's a pile of small, careful decisions, and I want to walk through
them one by one, in plain words. If you build apps with AI, they're worth knowing, because
they show how to think when you don't have much to work with.
Let's start with the problem. A language model reads text as tokens. A token might be
a whole word, a piece of a word, or just a punctuation mark. Tokens go in, the model's
answer comes back out as new tokens, and in between they pass through a lot of layers.
Two things make this hard on a phone. The first is space. At 16-bit precision,
3 billion parameters take up almost 6 gigabytes, and that's before anything else. The model also
needs room for your prompt, its calculations and temporary results, while the phone is still
running the operating system and your other apps out of the same memory. The model can't have the
whole house. The second is speed, or really how fast data can move. When the model writes text,
the processor keeps pulling numbers out of memory, again and again. Even a very fast chip ends up
waiting on them. It's like a lightning-fast chef with a slow helper bringing the ingredients.
The chef spends most of the day standing around. On top of that, the phone has to save battery,
stay cool, and keep every other app responsive. Nobody wants an AI feature that freezes the whole
phone. So those are the two walls. How much memory you have, and how fast you can move
data through it. Every trick from here on goes after one of them.
Trick 1. Make every number smaller. The most direct way to shrink a model is to use fewer
bits for each weight. That's called quantisation. Picture a box of a thousand crayons, each
one a slightly different shade, next to a box of just 16. You lose some subtle differences,
is, but the drawing still looks great. The hard part is finding the balance where you
save a lot of memory and the quality stays good.
Apple uses a kind of quantisation called palletisation. The name comes from a painter's palette,
but paint by number is an easier way to understand it.
In a paint by number picture, you don't write the colour name on every spot, you write
a small number like one, two or three, and a key at the bottom says which paint each
number means. Palatisation does the same thing with weights.
A lot of weights have nearly the same value, so you put them in groups. A small lookup table
holds one example value per group, and that table is the key. Each weight then stores just
a short note that points to a spot in the table.
How short can that note be? A bit is a zero or a one, so two bits give you four different
notes, enough to point to one of four table entries. Four bits give you sixteen. Compared
to a normal 16-bit number, a 2-bit note is 8 times smaller. In an earlier version of the model,
Apple mixed 2-bit and 4-bit notes, so some weights got 2 bits and others got 4. On average,
that came to 3.7 bits per weight. Let's run the numbers.
3 billion weights at 3.7 bits each is about 11.1 billion bits. Divide by 8 to get bytes,
and you land at roughly 1.39 gigabytes. Compare that to the almost 6 gigabytes we had at 16
bits. It's less than a quarter. So why mix sizes at all? Because not every part of a model is equally
sensitive. It's like packing a box. Socks can get squished flat, but a glass of ours needs a lot of
bubble wrap. Some parts of the model are socks. Napple squeezes those harder. Others are vases,
and they get more bits. The newer model goes further. The main decoder weights are down to
two bits each, and the embedding table uses four bits each.
The decoder is the main body of the model, the part that does the thinking and writes
the answer one token at a time. The embedding table works like a dictionary. You look up
a token and it gives you back a list of numbers the model can use.
There's a catch though. Rounding every number to a handful of choices is a big change. If
you do it after the model has finished learning, the small errors pile up and the answers
get worse. So Apple uses something called quantisation-aware training.
Instead of squeezing the model at the end, you squeeze it while it's still learning.
From the start, the model works with the small set of values it'll actually use.
It attempts its task, sees where it goes wrong, and its weights get nudged to fix those mistakes,
with the squeezing rules still in place. That loop repeats all through training.
It's like a drawing test where you only get four crayons. If you practice with a thousand and
switch on test day, your drawing comes out messy. If you practice with 4 the whole time,
you learn how to make a good picture anyway. For developers, that means you shouldn't shrink a
finished model and just hope it holds up. Train it knowing it's going to be shrunk.
Trick 2. Don't do the same homework twice. Small weights are only half of the memory story.
The model needs memory while it works, too. Say it's read a paragraph and started answering.
To guess the next token, it needs information from all the earlier ones.
If it redid every calculation from scratch each time, it would waste a huge amount of
work.
So it keeps a KV cache, short for Key Value Cache.
It's a notebook where the model writes down results it already worked out, so it can look
them up next time instead of recalculating.
But the notebook costs memory, and it gets bigger as the text gets longer.
A model's weights can fit just fine, and it can still run into trouble on a long
document because the notebook gets too fat. So now you've got two targets. Shrink the
weights and shrink the cash. For the cash, Apple uses cross-layer KV sharing. Instead
of every layer keeping its own notebooks, some layers share one. Imagine the model as
a building with eight floors. The bottom five each keep their own notes. The top three keep
none and just read the notes from floor five. That's three notebooks gone out of eight
8, and 3 over 8 is 0.375, so the cache uses 37.5% less memory. The lesson for developers
is to not stop at the weights when you plan memory. With long inputs, the cache matters
just as much.
Trick 3. One brain, many hats.
Compression makes one model smaller, but a phone needs a lot of different features. One
writes short notification summaries, another rewrites long text in a different style,
another pulls out key facts.
The lazy way is to build a separate model for every job, but they'd all share the same basic
language skills, so you'd be storing the same knowledge over and over. Adapters fix that.
An adapter is a small set of extra parameters that changes how the base model behaves for
one task. The base model is the actor, and the adapter is the costume. Same actor,
different hats. Adapters are built with a method called LoRa, short for low-rank adaptation. You
and train only those pieces for the new task. That's far cheaper than training or shipping
a whole new model. Each of Apple's adapters is only tens of megabytes, which is a tiny
fraction of the base model. On the phone, one base model stays in memory and the small adapters
get swapped in and out depending on the task. Trick 4. Keep the chips happy.
Even a small model needs a plan for the hardware. An iPhone has several kinds of processes. The
The GPU handles lots of number operations at the same time. The Apple Neural Engine runs
machine learning work efficiently. But you can't just point the model at one of them
and call it done. You still have to pick the right data layouts, split big arrays into pieces
that are easy to handle, and avoid extra memory copies.
It's a lot like moving boxes between rooms. Carry one at a time and copy each one along
the way, and it takes forever. Pack well and carry smart, and it goes fast. Those small
All choices change both speed and memory use. Trick 5. Know when to ask for help.
Even with all of that, the model on the phone has limits. And that's fine. The small model
is good at summarising, pulling out information, and sorting things into categories. When a
request comes in, Apple Intelligence first checks whether the phone can handle it.
If the job is harder, the request can go to Private Cloud Compute. Private Cloud Compute
is a protected space in the cloud. Only authorised software can process your data there, and
outside parties are blocked from seeing it. Your device encrypts the request for verified servers
and sends it over an encrypted connection. Any machine outside that boundary doesn't have the
keys to read it. The goal is that even Apple's own staff and admin systems can't see what's
in your request. Once it arrives, a separate, larger server model takes over. It uses
something called mixture of experts computation, along with parallel processing tracks. Put simply,
a big model can pick the best parts of itself for each job and spread the work around. So the system
has two gears. Do it on the phone when you can and call the cloud when you have to.
Now, what's new in 2026? Apple keeps updating these models. This year it launched AFM3 Core,
a new generation of the 3 billion parameter model, along with AFM3 Core Advanced.
Core Advanced is a sparse model. What does that mean? In a normal or dense model, every
parameter works on every token. A sparse model is split into lots of smaller specialist parts
called experts, and for each job it wakes up only the ones it needs. The rest just sit
idle. It's like a big hospital with hundreds of doctors. You only ever see the two or
three who match your problem.
Core Advanced has 20 billion parameters in total, but only one to four billion are active
at a time, depending on what the Apple Silicon system can handle. So you get the knowledge
of a big model at roughly the running cost of a small one.
The storage side is clever too. The full model lives on flash storage, and only the experts
your prompt needs get loaded into memory. The system doesn't swap experts in from
flash for every single token. Think of a huge library in the basement, with just
the few books you need sitting on your desk. The cloud side grew as well. Private cloud
compute workloads can now run on Nvidia GPUs in Google Cloud.
Zoom out and there's one idea underneath all of this. The model's power should match
the resources it has at runtime. A small phone gets a small squeezed model. A stronger device
can wake up more experts. A hard request can go to the cloud. No single model has to fit
every situation, so the system adapts. So what can you take from this for your own work? Here are
six things I'd remember. Know your two walls. Memory size and memory speed are separate problems
and you need to deal with both. Compress carefully. Spend more bits where the model is sensitive and
fewer where it's tough and train with the compression in mind. Watch the cache, not just
the weights. Long inputs can fill up memory even when the model is small. Share the base and
swap the hats. Adaptors let many features live on one foundation.
Match your code to the hardware. Layouts, chunking and fewer copies matter nearly as
much as the chip itself. And plan a fallback. Run locally first, go to the cloud only when
the job needs it, and protect the data on the way there. To wrap up, Apple didn't get a language
model onto an iPhone by finding one big secret. It got there by spotting waste and cutting it out,
– one piece at a time. Small awaits, a slimmer cache, a shared base with light adapters,
code built for the hardware, and a safe path to the cloud for when the phone needs help.
If you're building AI for limited devices, that's the takeaway. Before you ask for
a bigger device, go looking for what you're wasting.
